client: I've been having a really hard time since my dad passed away two months ago — it was so sudden, and I just wasn't prepared for it at all. Everything feels kind of grey and flat now, like I go through the motions of my day but nothing actually feels meaningful or enjoyable anymore. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd try because I don't know what else to do.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out, especially when part of you doubts it will help — and I want you to know that what you're feeling makes complete sense after losing your dad so suddenly and without any chance to prepare. That grey, flat feeling you're describing, where the color seems to have drained out of everyday life, is a very natural response to grief, not a sign that something is permanently broken in you. I'm really glad you're here, and I'd love to understand more — when you think about your dad, is there a particular moment or feeling that tends to come up most strongly for you?

client: I appreciate you saying that, but honestly, part of me still wonders if talking about it is just going to make it worse, you know? Like, the thing that keeps coming up is this image of the last time I saw him — we kind of had an argument about something stupid, and I never got to fix it. I just carry this feeling that he died thinking I didn't care about him, and I don't know how to get past that.
therapist: That weight you're carrying — the fear that he died with a wrong impression of you — sounds absolutely exhausting, and it makes so much sense that your mind keeps returning to that last moment. I want to gently ask you to consider this: in the full story of your relationship with your dad, across all the years you shared, is one argument really the thing that would have defined how he understood your love for him? When you think about who he was as a person, what do you imagine he actually held in his heart about you?

client: I want to believe what you're saying, I really do, but my mind just keeps snagging on that one moment. Like, logically I know we had years of good times, but in the middle of the night when I can't sleep, logic doesn't really show up. And honestly, I don't know what he held in his heart, because I never got to ask him, and that's the part that kills me.
therapist: That uncertainty — never getting the chance to ask him — is one of the most painful parts of sudden loss, and I don't want to minimize how real that ache is. What you're describing at 3am is actually something our minds do under grief and stress: they zero in on the most painful possibility as if it were fact, even when the full picture is much more complex. I'm wondering — if your dad were sitting here right now, and you could tell him what you wish he knew, what would you most want to say to him?

client: I sit with that question for a moment because it catches me off guard. I think... I'd want him to know that I'm sorry I wasn't there more in the last year, that I got so caught up in my own stuff and I just assumed we had more time. And I'd want him to know that I loved him even when I was bad at showing it, because I'm not sure he always knew that.
therapist: What you just shared is so tender and so honest, and the love in those words is unmistakable — the very fact that you carry this much pain is itself evidence of how deeply you cared. I also notice something important: you said you loved him "even when you were bad at showing it," which tells me you know the love was always there, even when life got in the way, and chances are he felt that too in ways that went beyond any single argument. I'm curious — is there anything you remember from your years together, maybe something small, that might suggest he did know you loved him, even imperfectly?

client: I sit with that for a moment, because honestly my first instinct is to brush it off and say "I don't know." But there is this one thing I keep coming back to — he used to call me on Sunday mornings just to talk about nothing, football scores or whatever he'd watched on TV, and he kept doing that even after some of our worst fights. Maybe that means something, I don't know, but it also just makes me sad because I didn't always pick up.
therapist: Those Sunday morning calls are so meaningful — he kept reaching for you, consistently, even after conflict, and that's not something people do unless they feel a fundamental connection and love. And I want to gently reflect something back to you: you remember those calls, you notice what they meant, and even the sadness you feel about the missed ones shows how much you valued that thread between you. What do you think it says about him — and about the two of you — that he kept calling?

client: I think it says he never stopped caring, even when things were hard between us... and maybe that he was more patient with me than I ever gave him credit for. But then I feel this wave of guilt, because if he kept reaching out and I wasn't always there, what does that say about me? I don't know if I can hold onto the idea that it was a real connection without also feeling like I failed it somehow.
therapist: The fact that you can hold both of those things — his patience and your own regret — actually shows a lot of emotional honesty and maturity, even if it feels painful right now. But I want to gently challenge the idea that imperfectly showing up to a relationship means you failed it — real connections aren't destroyed by missed calls or busy seasons of life, and his continued reaching out suggests he understood that too. I'm wondering, if a close friend described their relationship with their parent in exactly the same way you just described yours, would you tell them they had failed — or would you see something more complicated and more human than that?

client: I mean... no, I wouldn't tell a friend they failed. I'd probably say they did the best they could given everything going on in their life. But it feels different when it's me — like I'm supposed to hold myself to a higher standard because he was my dad, not just anyone.
therapist: What you just noticed is really important — that gap between the compassion you'd freely offer a friend and the much harsher standard you hold yourself to is something worth sitting with, because it tells us a lot about where some of this pain is coming from. That double standard isn't a sign that you're right to judge yourself more harshly; it's actually a very common pattern in grief, where love gets tangled up with self-blame as a way of trying to make sense of an unbearable loss. I'm curious — where do you think that belief comes from, that loving someone deeply means you're not allowed the same grace you'd give anyone else?

client: I don't know, I've never really thought about it that way before. I guess somewhere along the line I started believing that if I really loved him, I should have done more, seen the signs earlier, been there in a different way. It's like the love itself is what makes me feel like I failed him, and I'm not sure I can just... untangle that, even if what you're saying makes sense logically.
therapist: What you just articulated — that the love itself is the source of the guilt — is a really profound insight, and it makes so much sense that it feels impossible to untangle, because you've been carrying that belief for a long time without even knowing it was there. We don't have to untangle it all at once; just noticing that the guilt and the love have gotten knotted together is itself a meaningful first step, and it's something we can gently explore over time. I'm wondering — does any part of you believe that your dad, knowing you the way he did, would want you to keep punishing yourself with that knot, or would he want something different for you?

client: That question kind of stopped me in my tracks, because I know the answer — I know he wouldn't want this for me. But knowing that and actually feeling it are two completely different things, and right now it just feels like an intellectual answer I can give without it really landing anywhere inside me. It's like I can say the words "he'd want me to be okay" but there's still this other part that insists I don't deserve to be.
therapist: You just named something really important — that there's a part of you that doesn't feel you deserve to be okay, and that's worth taking seriously, because that belief is carrying a lot of weight right now. The gap between knowing something and *feeling* it is real, and it often takes time and gentle repetition before the heart catches up with what the mind already understands — so please don't judge yourself for being in that gap. I'm curious about that voice that says you don't deserve to be okay — how long do you think it's been with you, and do you sense it was there even before you lost your dad?

client: Honestly, that voice has been around for a long time... way before my dad died. I think it started when I was pretty young, like I always felt like I had to earn my place in the family, earn people's love, and if I messed up even a little it meant I wasn't good enough. Losing my dad just kind of turned up the volume on something that was already there, you know?
therapist: What you just shared takes real courage, and it reframes so much — your dad's death didn't create this wound, it reopened something much older, and that means the grief you're carrying is doing double duty right now. That young part of you who learned love had to be earned deserved so much better than that burden, and it makes complete sense that it's been shaping how you see yourself ever since. I'm wondering — when you think back to that younger version of you, the one who first learned they had to earn their place, what do you wish someone had told them?
